steps.say: Two steps. First the GPE at the top, then set it equal to KE to find the speed.

steps.done: Matches the GPE, so 14 m/s is right.

gold.display: A 3 kg rock falls from a height of 10 m. Calculate its speed just before it lands, assuming all GPE becomes KE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps.say: Kinetic energy needs the speed squared: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).

steps.done: That is the kinetic energy, 9 J.
Back to 3 m/s, so 9 J is right.

bronze.display: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

steps.say: The mass is in grams, but the equation needs kilograms. Convert first.

steps.done: 4 J. The only new move was the gram-to-kilogram conversion.

silver.display: A 500 g trolley moves at 4 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

steps.say: Two identical cars crash into a wall. Car A is going 15 mph. Car B is going 30 mph, exactly twice as fast.

steps.pre: Car B is travelling how many times as fast as Car A?

steps.say: You might guess the crash is twice as bad. It is worse than that. Energy depends on the speed squared, so doubling the speed multiplies the energy by 2 × 2.

Four times the energy, four times the damage. That squared speed is the heart of the kinetic energy equation, \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\). This lesson uses it alongside four partner equations for energy and power.

steps: Decide what you are finding, then choose the matching equation.
Convert every value to base units first: kg, metres, seconds.
State the answer with its unit (J for energy, W for power).
method_card.title: Energy: KE, GPE and Power
method_card.content:
Five recall equations: kinetic energy \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), gravitational PE \(E_p = mgh\), work \(W = Fs\), and power \(P = \frac{E}{t}\). Check whether your board gives you these; knowing them from memory always saves time.

Watch the traps: speed is squared, so doubling it quadruples the KE; convert grams to kilograms and minutes to seconds before substituting; use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg unless told otherwise.

steps: These need two equations or two stages. Finish the first fully before starting the second.
Energy is conserved: GPE lost becomes KE gained, so \(mgh = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\) lets you find a speed.
For efficiency, divide the useful energy by the total energy, then multiply by 100 for a percentage.
gold.title: Gold: two steps chained

example.question: A 2 kg ball falls from 10 m. Find its speed at the bottom. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: Pick the equation the quantity needs: kinetic energy \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\), gravitational PE \(E_p = mgh\), work \(W = Fs\), or power \(P = \frac{E}{t}\).
Substitute the numbers exactly as given, then calculate.
Write the answer with its unit: joules (J) for energy, watts (W) for power.
bronze.title: Bronze: one equation, straight in

example.question: A 4 kg box is lifted 3 m. Calculate the GPE gained. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

steps: If a value is not in the base unit, convert before you substitute: grams to kilograms (÷1000), minutes to seconds (×60), kilojoules to joules (×1000).
If the unknown is not the subject, rearrange the equation first, then substitute.
Give the answer in the unit the question asks for.
silver.title: Silver: convert first, or rearrange first

example.question: A 250 g ball moves at 6 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

exam_context.frequency: Very common. Energy calculations appear on almost every Paper 1.

gold.hint: Find the GPE lost over the 1000 m drop, then solve half m v squared for v.
gold.display: A skydiver of mass 75 kg falls from 4000 m to 3000 m. Calculate the speed they would reach if all the lost GPE converted to KE. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: All the lost GPE becomes KE. Find the GPE dropped, then solve \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\) for v.

guided_steps.hint: Double it, then divide by the mass.

guided_steps.done: Matches the GPE lost, so 140 m/s is right.

misconceptions.message: GPE lost = mgh = 75 × 9.8 × 1000 = 735,000 J. Set ½mv² = 735,000, so v² = 2 × 735,000 ÷ 75 = 19,600 and v = 140 m/s. Forgetting the 2 gives about 99 m/s.
Use the height dropped (4000 − 3000 = 1000 m), not the total 4000 m. Using 4000 m gives 280 m/s.

gold.hint: Work done is the kinetic energy lost: KE at 20 minus KE at 8.
gold.display: A car of mass 1100 kg travels at 20 m/s. The driver brakes, and the car decelerates to 8 m/s. Calculate the work done by the brakes.

guided_steps.say: Work done by the brakes is the KE lost: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\) before minus after.

guided_steps.hint: Subtract the smaller from the larger.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 220,000 J, so 184,800 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Add back to the starting KE.

misconceptions.message: Find the KE at both speeds and subtract: ½ × 1100 × 20² = 220,000 J and ½ × 1100 × 8² = 35,200 J, so work = 184,800 J. Squaring the difference (12²) gives 79,200 J, which is wrong.

gold.hint: Useful output is the GPE gained; total input is power times time.
gold.display: An electric motor has a power rating of 2.5 kW. It lifts an 80 kg object 6 m in 4 seconds. Calculate the efficiency of the motor. Give your answer as a percentage. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input × 100. Useful output is the GPE gained; total input is \(Pt\).

guided_steps.hint: Total input × the efficiency fraction recovers the useful output.

misconceptions.message: Convert kW to W: 2.5 kW = 2500 W, so total input = 2500 × 4 = 10,000 J. Leaving it as 2.5 gives a total input of 10 J and an impossible 47,040%.
Efficiency = useful ÷ total × 100 = 4704 ÷ 10,000 × 100 = 47.04%. Dividing total by useful instead gives about 212%.

gold.hint: Work out each student's power with mgh divided by time, then subtract.
gold.display: Two students climb the same flight of stairs (height 4 m). Student A has mass 50 kg and takes 5 seconds. Student B has mass 70 kg and takes 8 seconds. Calculate the difference in their power output. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Find each student's power with \(P = \frac{mgh}{t}\), then subtract.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 392 W, so 49 W is right.
guided_steps.hint: Add back to Student B's power.

misconceptions.message: Power, not energy: divide each student's work by their time. P_A = 1960 ÷ 5 = 392 W, P_B = 2744 ÷ 8 = 343 W, difference = 49 W. Comparing energies (2744 − 1960) gives 784.

gold.hint: Find the GPE before and after, then subtract.
gold.display: A ball of mass 0.3 kg is dropped from a height of 10 m. It bounces back to a height of 6 m. Calculate the energy dissipated during the bounce. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Energy dissipated is the GPE lost: mgh before the bounce minus mgh after.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 29.4 J, so 11.76 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Add back to the bounce GPE.

misconceptions.message: Energy dissipated is the GPE lost: mgh before minus mgh after = 29.4 − 17.64 = 11.76 J. Quoting only the starting GPE gives 29.4 J.

gold.hint: Convert MW to watts and one day to seconds, then multiply.
gold.display: A wind turbine generates 1.5 MW of power. How much energy does it transfer in one day? Give your answer in standard form.

guided_steps.say: Energy is \(E = Pt\). Convert the power to watts and one day to seconds first.

guided_steps.pre: In standard form, the power of 10 is
guided_steps.hint: Move the point 11 places left from 129,600,000,000.

guided_steps.pre: and the number in front (between 1 and 10) is
guided_steps.hint: Put the decimal after the first digit.

bronze.hint: Square the speed, then multiply by half the mass.
bronze.display: A car has a mass of 1200 kg and travels at 15 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy needs the speed squared: \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2\).

guided_steps.done: Back to 15 m/s, so 135,000 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed first: 15² = 225. Then KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J.
Do not forget the ½. KE = ½ × 1200 × 225 = 135,000 J, not 270,000 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply mass by g, then by height.
bronze.display: A 0.5 kg ball is held 4 m above the ground. Calculate its gravitational potential energy. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Lifting something gives it gravitational PE: \(E_p = mgh\).

guided_steps.done: Gives 9.8 N/kg, so 19.6 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide back by height then mass.

misconceptions.message: Use GPE = mgh = 0.5 × 9.8 × 4 = 19.6 J. This is a mass held above the ground, so it stores gravitational PE, not KE.

bronze.hint: Work done is force times distance.
bronze.display: A force of 50 N pushes a box 8 m along the floor. Calculate the work done.

guided_steps.say: Work done is force times distance: \(W = Fs\).

guided_steps.done: Recovers 50 N, so 400 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Work done = force × distance = 50 × 8 = 400 J.

bronze.hint: Convert minutes to seconds, then divide energy by time.
bronze.display: A kettle transfers 180,000 J of energy in 3 minutes. Calculate its power in watts.

guided_steps.say: Power is energy per second: \(P = \frac{E}{t}\). Time must be in seconds.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 180,000 J, so 1000 W is right.

misconceptions.message: Convert minutes to seconds first: 3 min = 180 s. P = 180,000 ÷ 180 = 1000 W. Dividing by 3 gives 60,000 W, which is far too big.

bronze.hint: Square the speed, then multiply by half the mass.
bronze.display: A runner of mass 60 kg sprints at 8 m/s. Calculate their kinetic energy.

guided_steps.done: Back to 8 m/s, so 1920 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Square the speed: 8² = 64. KE = ½ × 60 × 64 = 1920 J. Forgetting to square gives 240 J.

bronze.hint: Multiply mass by g, then by height.
bronze.display: A bag of mass 3 kg is lifted onto a shelf 2.5 m high. Calculate the GPE gained. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.done: Gives 9.8 N/kg, so 73.5 J is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide back by height then mass.

bronze.hint: Divide the energy by the time.
bronze.display: A motor does 5000 J of work in 20 seconds. Calculate its power.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 5000 J, so 250 W is right.

misconceptions.message: Power = energy ÷ time = 5000 ÷ 20 = 250 W. Multiplying instead gives 100,000, which is not a power.

bronze.hint: Above the ground means gravitational potential energy.
bronze.display: Which equation would you use to calculate the energy stored by an object lifted above the ground?

misconceptions.message: An object above the ground has gravitational PE. Use \(E_p = mgh\). KE is for moving objects.

silver.hint: Work out the KE in joules, then convert to kilojoules.
silver.display: A cyclist and bike have a combined mass of 80 kg and travel at 12 m/s. Calculate the kinetic energy in kJ.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy in joules first, then convert to kilojoules.

guided_steps.done: Recovers 5760 J, so 5.76 kJ is right.

misconceptions.message: KE = ½ × 80 × 12² = 5760 J. The question asks for kJ: 5760 ÷ 1000 = 5.76 kJ.
Square the speed first: 12² = 144. Then ½ × 80 × 144 = 5760 J = 5.76 kJ. Forgetting to square gives 0.48 kJ.

silver.hint: Convert hours to seconds, then convert the answer to kJ.
silver.display: A 60 W light bulb is left on for 2 hours. Calculate the energy transferred in kJ.

guided_steps.say: Energy transferred: \(E = Pt\). Time in seconds, then convert joules to kilojoules.

guided_steps.done: Gives 60 W, so 432 kJ is right.
guided_steps.hint: Divide the joules by the time.

misconceptions.message: Convert hours to seconds: 2 h = 7200 s. E = 60 × 7200 = 432,000 J = 432 kJ. Leaving the answer in joules gives 432,000.

silver.hint: Find the weight first, then multiply by the height.
silver.display: A crane lifts a 400 kg load to a height of 15 m. Calculate the work done by the crane. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Work against gravity: first the weight \(W = mg\), then work \(W = Fs\).

guided_steps.done: Recovers 3920 N, so 58,800 J is right.

misconceptions.message: First find the weight to lift: W = mg = 400 × 9.8 = 3920 N. Then work = Fs = 3920 × 15 = 58,800 J. Using the mass as the force gives 6000 J.

silver.hint: Work done equals the kinetic energy gained from rest.
silver.display: A car of mass 900 kg accelerates from rest to 30 m/s. Calculate the work done on the car.

guided_steps.say: Work done equals the KE gained: \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\), since it starts from rest.

guided_steps.done: Back to 30 m/s, so 405,000 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Work done = the KE gained = ½ × 900 × 30² = 405,000 J. It starts from rest, so there is no KE to subtract.
Square the speed: 30² = 900. KE = ½ × 900 × 900 = 405,000 J. Forgetting to square gives 13,500 J.

silver.hint: Find the energy from Pt, then rearrange mgh to h = E divided by mg.
silver.display: A 1500 W motor lifts a 50 kg mass. How high can it lift the mass in 10 seconds? Give your answer to 1 d.p. (g = 9.8 N/kg)

guided_steps.say: Two equations: energy in from \(E = Pt\), then height from \(E_p = mgh\) rearranged to \(h = \frac{E}{mg}\).

guided_steps.done: About 15,000 J, so 30.6 m is right.
guided_steps.hint: Weight × height recovers the energy, close to 15,000.

misconceptions.message: Energy = Pt = 15,000 J. Height = E ÷ (mg) = 15,000 ÷ 490 = 30.6 m. Dividing by the mass alone (forgetting g) gives 300 m.

silver.hint: Convert the mass to kilograms first, then square the speed.
silver.display: A 200 g tennis ball is served at 50 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

guided_steps.say: Kinetic energy: convert the mass to kilograms first.

guided_steps.done: Back to 50 m/s, so 250 J is right.

misconceptions.message: Convert grams to kilograms: 200 g = 0.2 kg. KE = ½ × 0.2 × 50² = 250 J. Leaving the mass in grams gives 250,000 J.

problem_bank.gold_description: Chain two steps: convert energy between GPE and KE, find work from a change in KE, or work out an efficiency or a difference.
problem_bank.bronze_description: One equation, all values already in the right units. Recall it, substitute, and calculate.
problem_bank.silver_description: Convert a unit first (grams to kilograms, minutes to seconds, joules to kilojoules) or rearrange the equation before you substitute.
